5.2

# Congressional Enforcement of Civil Rights Under Civil War Amendments: Introduction

# Introduction to Congressional Enforcement of Civil Rights Under Civil War Amendments

The Civil Rights Amendments (13th, 14th and 15th), which were passed after the Civil War each contain an enforcement clause empowering Congress to enforce the Amendments.

Each Amendment contains the following language: “The Congress shall have power to enforce, by appropriate legislation, the provisions of this article.”

You studied these powers in Liberty, Equality and Due Process (LEDP). Below is a short recap to this set of powers.

The Civil War Amendments, the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments, were designed to address the evils of slavery, racial inequality and discrimination.

The 13th Amendment prohibits slavery and involuntary servitude. The 14th Amendment establishes that all people born and naturalized in the United States are citizens and that no state can abridge the privileges and immunities of U.S. citizens. The Amendment also provides that no state may deprive any person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law or deny any person equal protection of the laws. The 15th Amendment states: “The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.”

The 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments do not require subsequent legislation to be directly
enforceable. Nonetheless, Congress has passed various forms of legislation under the Enforcement Clauses each of these Amendments.

These Amendments, and particularly section 5 of the 14th Amendment, serve as a basis on which Congress may abrogate 11th Amendment immunity.

It should be noted that the 13th Amendment applies to everyone, be they a state actor or a private person, while the letter of the 14th Amendment limits its application to the state.

The Court has interpreted the 13th Amendment enforcement provision to include not only slavery and indentured servitude, but also the badges and incidents of slavery. The Court was very deferential to Congress during the 1960s and 1970s and applied a rational basis test to Congress’s determination that it was addressing a badge or incident of slavery. This deferential approach to the Enforcement Clause of the 13th Amendment has not really been tested before the Supreme Court since the 70s and so it is somewhat difficult to predict how the present Court would address those powers.

The Court was also deferential to Congress during the 60s and 70s when it came to the 14th Amendment’s enforcement clause, but in keeping with the spirit of the 1990s (see Commerce Clause Powers), the Court became less deferential, holding that Congress cannot reinterpret rights or expand rights beyond the scope determined by the Supreme Court. In City of Boerne v. Flores (1997) the Court held that “[t]here must be a congruence and proportionality between the injury to be prevented or remedied and the means adopted to that end.”

The test under the 15th Amendment enforcement clause was whether Congress had a rational basis for determining that the law was an appropriate mechanism for enforcing the Amendment. However, in the Court's recent decision, Shelby v. Holder (2013), it used the less deferential test of “sufficiently related.” The use of this new test is due in part a finding that sections of the Voting Rights Act violated states equal sovereignty.

The Court, found that the section 4 list of jurisdictions that were required to get pre-clearance from federal government before they made changes to their voting procedures, was outdated, not justified by present conditions, and that it offended the equal sovereignty of states. Because the Act did not treat states equally, the Court required the disparate geographic coverage to be “sufficiently related to the problem” that was targeted. The Court found that it was not.

5.2.1

# Immunity for Governmental Entities - Congruent and Proportionality Test - Limit on Congress

2 Federal Civil Rights Acts (3d ed.) § 14:83 Federal Civil Rights Acts | March 2022 Update Rodney A. Smolla

Chapter 14. Deprivation of Rights Under Color of Law: § 1983, Bivens Actions, and Related Issues

14:83. Immunities for governmental entities—The complex matrix of modern Eleventh Amendment law—§ 1983 is not a general override as applied to states—The congruence and proportionality test

In Kimel v. Florida Board of Regents,1 the Supreme Court ruled that state employees cannot bring an action in federal court against the state under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (”ADEA”). The Court held that the ADEA contained a clear statement of Congress’s intent to abrogate the states’ Eleventh Amendment immunity from suit in federal court by private individuals, but the purported abrogation exceeded Congress’s authority under § 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The ADEA prohibits employment discrimination against individuals because of their age if they are over forty. The ADEA also provides that an employee can maintain a suit against a public agency in any federal or state court of competent jurisdiction. A public agency includes the government of a state or its political subdivision and any agency of a state of its public subdivision. Several current and former state employees of Alabama and Florida filed suit against their state employers for violations under the ADEA.2

Justice O’Connor authored the 5–4 majority opinion, first noting the established principle that the Eleventh Amendment prohibits federal jurisdiction over suits against nonconsenting states. Congress can, however, abrogate the states’ Eleventh Amendment immunity in a federal statute by “makings its intention unmistakably clear in the language of the statute.”3 The Court held that the ADEA satisfied this test by incorporating provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act (”FLSA”) that provide specifically for suits by individuals against states in courts of competent jurisdiction.4

Justice O’Connor then discussed the source of constitutional validity for the ADEA. Previously, the Court had found the ADEA valid under Congress’s Commerce Clause power.5 Subsequently, the Court held that Congress lacks power under Article I to abrogate the states’ sovereign immunity.6 Based on this precedent, the majority determined that “if the ADEA rests solely on Congress’s Article I commerce power, the private petitioners in today’s cases cannot maintain their suits against their state employers.”7

The Court recognized, however, that since § 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment grants Congress the authority to abrogate the states’ sovereign immunity, the petitioners’ actions could be maintained if the ADEA was appropriate under § 5.

The majority found that the power given to Congress in § 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment is to enforce the Amendment: “Congress can remedy and deter violation of the rights guaranteed by prohibiting a “broader swath of conduct.”8 The Court stated, however, that this power does not include the power to determine what constitutes constitutional violations; that power is left to the judiciary. The Court then used its prior decision in City of Boerne v. Flores9 to enunciate a test to determine when a statute falls within Congress’s § 5 powers: “there must be congruence and proportionality between the injury to be prevented or remedied and the means adopted to that end.”10

Applying the congruence and proportionality test, the Court concluded that the ADEA was not appropriate legislation under § 5. The Court determined that “[a]ge classifications, unlike governmental conduct based on race and gender, cannot be characterized as ‘so seldom relevant to the achievement of any legitimate state interest that laws grounded in such considerations are deemed to reflect prejudice and antipathy.’ ”11 The Court said that age is not a suspect class because “[o]ld age does not define a discrete and insular minority because all persons, if they live out their normal life spans, will experience it.”12 Therefore, the Constitution permits states to “draw lines on the basis of age when they have a rational basis for doing so at a class-based level, even if it is ‘probably not true’ that those reasons are valid in the majority of cases.”13 The Court interpreted the ADEA to mandate a broad restriction on the use of age in making employment decisions; therefore, it prohibits many more state employment practices than would be held unconstitutional under the rational basis standard.

The Court also declined to apply the ADEA to the states because, after an examination of the Act’s legislative history, it found that Congress never identified a pattern and practice of age discrimination by the states, much less discrimination that rose to levels that would offend the Constitution. The Court determined that even though age discrimination may have been a problem in isolated circumstances or in isolated states, it was not a problem of national import. The Court also declined to treat evidence of discrimination in the private sector as indicative of discrimination in the public sector.

Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Souter, Justice Ginsburg, and Justice Breyer, dissented in part and concurred in part. Justice Stevens agreed that Congress clearly expressed its intent to subject states to suits by private parties under the ADEA, but disagreed regarding the majority’s Eleventh Amendment analysis. Justice Stevens expressed the view that Congress’s power to authorize federal remedies against state agencies that violate federal statutory obligations is coextensive with Congress’s power to impose those obligations on the states, and that neither the Eleventh Amendment nor the doctrine of sovereign immunity places any limit on that power. Justice Stevens disagreed with the applicability of Seminole Tribe and asserted that it was wrongly decided. He further opined that “[i]t cannot be maintained that a State’s ordering of its affairs with respect to potential liability under federal law requires adherence to Seminole Tribe, as that decision leaves open a State’s liability upon enforcement of federal law by federal remedies.”14

The Supreme Court again applied the congruence and proportionality principles in Board of Trustees of the University of Alabama v. Garrett,15 holding that states enjoy Eleventh Amendment immunity from the coverage of the ADA.16 The case involved two Alabama state employees, who sought money damages against their employer, the state of Alabama, for alleged violations of the ADA.17 In a 5–4 decision written by Chief Justice Rehnquist, the Supreme Court held that application of the ADA against the states violated the Eleventh Amendment. The disabled, the Court held, do not constitute a “suspect” or a “quasi-suspect” class, triggering “strict scrutiny” or “intermediate scrutiny” review when they are discriminated against.18 While the disabled may be subject to some irrational biases in our society, the Court reasoned, that alone does not make them a suspect or quasi-suspect class.19 States are thus not required by the Fourteenth Amendment to make special accommodations for the disabled, so long as their actions towards such individuals are rational.20 In tough-minded language, the Court concluded that the states “could quite hardheadedly—and perhaps hardheartedly—hold to job-qualification requirements which do not make allowance for the disabled.”21

The legislative record compiled by Congress when enacting the ADA failed to show that Congress identified a pattern of irrational state discrimination in employment against the disabled, the Court found, and thus did not support abrogation of the states’ Eleventh Amendment immunity from suits for money damages under Title I of the ADA.22 The Court was not willing to allow Congress to build its record based on acts of discrimination by local government.23 Lastly, the Court held that the expansive rights and remedies created by the ADA against the states raised concerns as to congruence and proportionality, further supporting the determination that Congress did not validly abrogate the states’ immunity. “Even were it possible to squeeze out of these examples a pattern of unconstitutional discrimination by the States, the rights and remedies created by the ADA against the States would raise the same sort of concerns as to congruence and proportionality as were found in City of Boerne,”24 the Court stated. The Court thus reasoned that while it would be entirely rational (and therefore constitutional) for a state employer to conserve scarce financial resources by hiring employees who are able to use existing facilities, the ADA requires employers to make existing facilities used by employees readily accessible to and usable by individuals with disabilities.25 While it is true that the ADA does except employers from the reasonable accommodation requirement where the employer can demonstrate that the accommodation would impose an undue hardship on the operation of the business, the Court held, “even with this exception, the accommodation duty far exceeds what is constitutionally required in that it makes unlawful a range of alternate responses that would be reasonable but would fall short of imposing an ‘undue burden’ upon the employer.”26

That the ADA extends to standards, criteria, or methods of administration that merely disparately impact on the disabled was another factor against the constitutionality of the law as applied to the states, the Court held, for this standard is applied by the law “without regard to whether such conduct has a rational basis.”27 Although disparate impact may be relevant evidence of racial discrimination, the Court reasoned, such evidence alone is insufficient to establish a violation of the Constitution, even where the Fourteenth Amendment subjects state action to the demanding test of strict scrutiny.28

”Congress is the final authority as to desirable public policy,” the Court concluded,” but in order to authorize private individuals to recover money damages against the States, there must be a pattern of discrimination by the States which violates the Fourteenth Amendment, and the remedy imposed by Congress must be congruent and proportional to the targeted violation.”29

In Tennessee v. Lane,30 a group of plaintiffs who were paraplegics filed an action for damages and equitable relief under Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, which provides that “no qualified individual with a disability shall, by reason of such disability, be excluded from participation or denied the benefits of the services, programs or activities of a public entity.”31 The case came in the wake of the Supreme Court’s decision in Board of Trustees of University of Alabama v. Garrett,32 in which the Supreme Court held that the Eleventh Amendment bars private money damages actions for state violations of Title I of the ADA, which prohibits employment discrimination against the disabled.

The Supreme Court in Tennessee v. Lane33 distinguished Garrett, holding that as it applies to the class of cases implicating the fundamental right of access to the courts, Title II constituted a valid exercise of the authority Congress possesses under § 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment to enforce the substantive rights guaranteed under the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Court found in Lane that Congress had abrogated the states’ Eleventh Amendment immunity. This inquiry the Court noted, requires resolution of two predicate questions: (1) whether Congress unequivocally expressed its intent to abrogate; and (2), if so, whether it acted pursuant to a valid grant of constitutional authority.34 The Court held that the first question was easily answered, since the ADA specifically provides for abrogation.35 With regard to the second question, the Court held, Congress can abrogate state sovereign immunity pursuant to a valid exercise of its power under § 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment.36 The abrogation power is not, however, unlimited. While Congress must have a wide berth in devising appropriate remedial and preventative measures for unconstitutional actions, the Court noted, those measures may not work a substantive change in the governing law.37

In City of Boerne v. Flores,38 the Court set forth the test for distinguishing between permissible remedial legislation and unconstitutional substantive redefinition. Section 5 legislation is valid if it exhibits “a congruence and proportionality” between an injury and the means adopted to prevent or remedy it.39 In Garrett, the Court concluded that Title I of ADA was not a valid exercise of Congress § 5 power under this test, because the historical record and the commodious sweep of the law suggested that real aim of Title I was not so much enforcement, but revision of the substantive law of the Fourteenth Amendment jurisprudence.

In Lane, however, the Court found important differences between the ADA’s Title I and Title II.40 Particularly when applied to the context of access to courthouse facilities, Title II appeared to enforce protections of a fundamental right-the right of access to the courts.41 The issue of whether Title II validly enforced these constitutional rights, the Court held, was a question that “must be judged with reference to the historical experience which it reflects.”42 Applying this test, the Court in Lane held that Title II of the ADA was indeed a valid exercise of Congress’ § 5 enforcement power.43 The historical experience that Title II reflects was documented in many court decisions, the Court noted, which had identified unconstitutional treatment of disabled persons by state agencies in a variety of public programs and services.44 The findings by Congress in the ADA that discrimination against individuals with disabilities persists in such critical areas as access to public services, the Court held, when coupled with the extensive record of disability discrimination that underlies it, made it clear that inadequate provision of public services and access to public facilities was an appropriate subject for prophylactic legislation.45 Title II was an appropriate response to this history and pattern of unequal treatment, the Court held. The law was clearly valid as it applied to the class of cases implicating the accessibility of judicial services. The remedy selected by Congress for the pattern of exclusion and discrimination at issue, the requirement of program accessibility, was congruent and proportional to the law’s object of enforcing the right of access to the courts.46 The long history of unequal treatment of disabled persons in the administration of judicial services has persisted despite several state and federal legislative efforts to remedy the problem, the Court noted. Faced with considerable evidence of the shortcomings of these previous efforts, Congress was justified in concluding that the difficult and intractable problem of disability discrimination warranted added prophylactic measures.47

The Court did emphasize that the remedy Congress chose was constrained and limited. Recognizing that failure to accommodate persons with disabilities will often have the same practical effect as outright exclusion, Congress required the States to take reasonable measures to remove architectural and other barriers to accessibility. But Title II does not require States to employ any and all means to make judicial services accessible or to compromise essential eligibility criteria for public programs. It requires only “reasonable modifications” that would not fundamentally alter the nature of the service provided, and only when the individual seeking modification is otherwise eligible for the service;48 and indeed, the law’s implementing regulations make clear that the reasonable modification requirement can be satisfied in various ways, including less costly measures than structural changes.49 This duty to accommodate is perfectly consistent with the well-established due process principle that, within the limits of practicability, a State must afford to all individuals a meaningful opportunity to be heard in its courts.50 Judged against this backdrop, the Court held Title II’s affirmative obligation to accommodate is a reasonable prophylactic measure, reasonably targeted to a legitimate end.51

In Coleman v. Court of Appeals of Maryland,52 the Supreme Court again applied the congruence and proportionality test. The power granted to Congress under § 5 of the 14th Amendment, the Court noted, “‘includes the authority both to remedy and to deter violation[s] of rights guaranteed’” by the § 1 of the Amendment.53 In order to ensure that when Congress employs § 5 it is genuinely engaged in “enforcement” and not in expansion of the substantive scope of the 14th Amendment, Congress “must tailor” legislation enacted under § 5 “‘to remedy or prevent’” “conduct transgressing the Fourteenth Amendment’s substantive provisions.”54 Under this test courts must consider the evil or wrong that Congress seeks to remedy, as well as the means employed to address the problem.55 The Court in Coleman emphasized that the legislation enacted by Congress pursuant to § 5 must be targeted at the constitutional violation, and there must be a “‘congruence and proportionality between the injury to be prevented or remedied and the means adopted to that end.’”56 While Hibbs sustained congressional power on a record of a well-documented pattern of sex-based discrimination in family-leave policies, the Court held, no similar patter supported a requirement that States give all employees the opportunity to take self-care leave.57 “Without widespread evidence of sex discrimination or sex stereotyping in the administration of sick leave, it is apparent that the congressional purpose in enacting the self-care provision is unrelated to these supposed wrongs,”58 the Court reasoned. “The legislative history of the self-care provision reveals a concern for the economic burdens on the employee and the employee’s family resulting from illness-related job loss and a concern for discrimination on the basis of illness, not sex.”59 The Court in Coleman also rejected the argument that the FMLA provision could be justified as a necessary adjunct to the family-care provisions.60 So too, the Court rejected the argument that the self-care provision could be justified because it helps single parents retain their jobs when they become ill. Whether or not this is true, the Court held, it “does not explain how the provision remedies or prevents constitutional violations.”61 On this point the Court noted that mere disparate impact on women is not enough to prove a 14th Amendment violation.62 “To the extent, then, that the self-care provision addresses neutral leave policies with a disparate impact on women, it is not directed at a pattern of constitutional violations.”63
